clue.text: London author to shoot pool

parts.note: Jack London was the American author of The Call of the Wild
to shoot or pot an animal is to kill it with a gun

explanation.surface: An author from London sets off to shoot a game of pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'London' looks like the city but is the surname of the novelist Jack London. A jackpot is a pool of money in a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A pool of accumulated stakes waiting to be won is a synonym, as in a lottery's prize fund.

clue.text: Flier when grounded creates motoring hazard

parts.note: a jay is a bird, something that flies
a bird on the ground goes on foot, so it becomes one who walks

explanation.surface: A bird on the ground makes trouble for drivers.
explanation.walkthrough: A jay that has to walk becomes a pedestrian crossing carelessly.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestrian crossing the road carelessly against traffic endangers drivers.

clue.text: Sort of pigeon that may spread disease?

explanation.surface: A kind of pigeon that may pass on illness.
explanation.walkthrough: Pigeons are often blamed for spreading disease, which binds the two senses together.
explanation.definitionFit: A homing bird used to take messages, and a person who transmits infection without symptoms.

clue.text: Principle that's basic, universal, in letters recently

indicators.note: in means the abbreviation for universal sits inside the other letters

parts.note: post is mail, letters delivered
late means recently, as in of late
U is the film-rating abbreviation for universal

explanation.surface: A fundamental universal rule shown in recent correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film certificate for 'universal' audiences.
explanation.definitionFit: A postulate is an assumption taken as a starting point for reasoning, a basic premise.

clue.text: Friar most liked by the fat boy of Greyfriars

definitions.text: most liked by the fat boy of Greyfriars

explanation.surface: A friar is the favourite of the plump schoolboy at Greyfriars.
explanation.walkthrough: Friar Tuck is Robin Hood's companion; Billy Bunter, the fat boy of Greyfriars School in British comics, loved food, in schoolboy slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Hood's jolly monk, and old British schoolboy slang for sweets and snacks that Bunter craved.

clue.text: Note about one such variety of ' flower

indicators.note: about means going around, so the musical note wraps the other letters

parts.note: fa is the fourth note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: a variety of something is a different version of it, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A note describing one particular kind of flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety of' turns SUCH into UCHS, and 'about' puts the note around it and the numeral. The flower is named after the botanist Fuchs.
explanation.definitionFit: The fuchsia is a shrub grown for its drooping red and purple blooms.

clue.text: Two by two — very firm and solid

explanation.surface: Two by two makes something steady and strong.
explanation.walkthrough: Two times two is four, giving four squared figuratively in a grid of two by two.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-by-two grid has four cells, and foursquare means steady and unshakeable.

clue.text: Madden with rage

explanation.surface: Driving someone mad with fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is only a link; 'rage' is the noun for a fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: To craze is to drive insane, and a rage is a passing fad or fashion.

clue.text: Do pigs go about 500.pounds?

indicators.note: go about means the word for pigs surrounds the other letters

parts.note: swine are pigs
D is the Roman numeral for 500
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Do pigs trot around costing five hundred pounds?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is not a question word but the verb meaning cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone is slang for cheating them out of money.

clue.text: A pressure of steam needed to move in this direction

parts.note: a head of steam is a built-up pressure in an engine

explanation.surface: Some steam pressure is required to move an engine along.
explanation.walkthrough: A head of steam is the pressure built up in a boiler.
explanation.definitionFit: Ahead means forwards, the direction of travel in front.

clue.text: Two — yes, about that — needed to make a battle

indicators.note: the word yes is placed about, that is around, the pair abbreviation

parts.note: taken as written
PR is the standard abbreviation for pair, a set of two

explanation.surface: Two people agreeing about something needed to start a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: PR, short for pair, stands for 'Two'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ypres in Belgium was the site of several major First World War battles.

clue.text: Unusually active outside America, producing effects

indicators.note: outside means the rearranged letters surround the abbreviation for America
something done unusually is done in an odd way, so the letters of active are rearranged

parts.note: USA is the abbreviation for the United States of America

explanation.surface: Someone unusually busy abroad is having an impact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusually' rearranges ACTIVE into CATIVE, which goes 'outside' USA: CA-USA-TIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something causative brings results about, acting as their cause.

clue.text: Hostility shown if one amount is rejected

parts.note: an is an archaic word for if, as in Shakespeare
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the word for amount is read backwards

parts.note: a sum is an amount of money

explanation.surface: Ill-feeling is displayed when a single sum of money is refused.
explanation.walkthrough: AN for 'if' is an old usage solvers meet often; 'is rejected' turns SUM into MUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Animus means ill will or antagonism toward someone, a close synonym of enmity.

clue.text: Rose has article that is finished

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
sc is short for Latin scilicet, meaning that is or namely
ended means finished or over

explanation.surface: A rose bush comes with an item that is now complete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like the flower but is the past tense of rise. SC (scilicet) is the less familiar abbreviation for 'that is', beside the usual IE.
explanation.definitionFit: To have climbed or gone up is a synonym for rose, the past tense of rise.

clue.text: Not drinking is to me out of order in a public conveyance

indicators.note: in means the rearranged letters go inside the vehicle

parts.note: a bus is public transport

indicators.note: out of order means not in their proper arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Being teetotal is wrong to me on a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not drinking' looks like it should describe a person but stands alone as the definition; 'out of order' shuffles IS TO ME into STEMIO.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstemious means sparing with food and especially alcohol.

clue.text: A mark could be a lot for a Buddhist to earn

definitions.text: a lot for a Buddhist to earn

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters might form something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A grade might be quite a lot for a Buddhist student to achieve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges A MARK. 'Lot' means one's fate, not a large amount.
explanation.definitionFit: In Buddhism karma is the destiny a person builds up through their actions, a fate earned by deeds.

clue.text: Unlimited advice to over-energetic kangaroos?

explanation.surface: A tip for kangaroos that are far too lively.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as BOUND LESS, the second reading tells kangaroos to jump less.
explanation.definitionFit: Boundless means without limit, while bound-less would urge a leaping animal to hop less often.

clue.text: In death sat up, requiring a little coffee,

indicators.note: in means one piece sits inside the word for death

parts.note: demise means death

indicators.note: in a down clue up means read from bottom to top, so sat is backwards

explanation.surface: In death someone sat up and asked for a small coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns SAT into TAS, which goes 'In' DEMISE.
explanation.definitionFit: A demitasse is a small cup of black coffee, French for half-cup.

clue.text: Late course of vegetables or flowers

parts.note: sweet is the dessert, a course late in a meal
peas are vegetables

explanation.surface: A final course of greens or blooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late course' is the dessert, called the sweet in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: These scented climbing garden plants grow colourful blooms.

clue.text: Cat's-eye as a type of telescope

explanation.surface: A road stud is likened to a kind of telescope.
explanation.walkthrough: A cat's-eye is a British road stud that shines back in headlights.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat's-eye bounces headlight beams back to drivers, and one class of telescope uses a mirror to gather light.

clue.text: Sound of trumpets announcing cost of eg. football excursion ticket?

definitions.text: cost of eg. football excursion ticket?

explanation.surface: Trumpets blare announcing what a football supporter pays for travel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'announcing' links the two; the second sense splits as FAN FARE.
explanation.definitionFit: A flourish of brass marks an entrance, and a supporter's travel charge is a fan's fare.

clue.text: Bishop seen in this joint

explanation.surface: A bishop is spotted in this pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joint' suggests a dive or bar, but here it is a carpentry joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop wears this tall pointed headdress, and a carpenter's corner joint is cut at forty-five degrees.

clue.text: One's early years generate outright revolution

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the remaining letters are rearranged
read as out right, it tells the solver to take the R for right out of generate

explanation.surface: Youthful years produce a full-scale uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outright' splits as 'out' plus 'right': R leaves GENERATE, leaving GENEATE, which 'revolution' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: The years from thirteen to nineteen are a person's adolescence.

clue.text: Drunkenness of this law-man angered monsieur?

indicators.note: drunkenness makes things reel and stagger, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for the French title monsieur

explanation.surface: A drunken French policeman upsets a gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunkenness' rearranges ANGERED plus M (monsieur); a policeman in France fits the French title.
explanation.definitionFit: A gendarme is a French police officer, an enforcer of the law.

clue.text: Works foreman almost makes a blunder

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a gaffer is a British word for a works foreman or boss

explanation.surface: A factory boss nearly commits a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: GAFFER is British slang for a foreman or boss.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaffe is a social blunder, an embarrassing slip.

clue.text: Freeborn lioness holds one up in the bridal path

indicators.note: holds means the reversed name contains the numeral
in a down clue up means the name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Elsa was the lioness of the book and film Born Free
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A lioness born free holds one up on a wedding path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freeborn' points to Born Free; 'up' turns ELSA into ASLE, which 'holds' I.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride walks down the central passage of the church between the pews.

clue.text: One as broad as another's high in Oxford

definitions.text: One as broad as another's high in Oxford

parts.words: One as broad as another's high in Oxford
parts.note: Oxford has a thoroughfare called Broad and another called the High, so the clue describes a kind of road

explanation.surface: In Oxford one thing is as wide as another is tall.
explanation.walkthrough: Broad Street and High Street are both famous Oxford roads; 'broad' and 'high' are names, not dimensions.
explanation.definitionFit: Broad and High are both names of Oxford thoroughfares, each a road lined with buildings.

clue.text: Some part extracted by a preacher from the Bible

definitions.text: Some part extracted by a preacher from the Bible

indicators.note: some means only a portion of the following words is used, so the letters lie within them

explanation.surface: A preacher pulls a passage out of scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: 'Some' points to letters inside PART EXTRACTED, and a preacher's sermon starts from a scripture passage.
explanation.definitionFit: A sermon is built on a short scriptural passage, the verse the preacher expounds.

clue.text: Standard weight of paving material

parts.note: a standard is a flag or banner
a stone is a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: The usual weight of material for a pavement.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat slab used for paths and floors is what this is.

clue.text: Typists use this bar room

explanation.surface: Typists drink at this bar room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar room' reads as a pub, but the bar belongs with the typists and 'room' is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: The long key on a keyboard puts gaps between words, and room means available area.

clue.text: One on each side of each of these sides

definitions.text: One on each side of each of these sides

parts.words: One on each side of each of these sides
parts.note: the number written as figures has a digit one on either side, and cricket or football teams are made of that many players

explanation.surface: Something with one on either side, of each of these teams.
explanation.walkthrough: Written in figures, the number has a 1 on each side; and teams of that size are called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Football and cricket teams each field this many players, so teams are named after the number.

clue.text: Pronouns provide Greek hero with a clue

parts.note: these is a demonstrative pronoun
us is a personal pronoun

explanation.surface: Grammar words hand a hero of Greece a hint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clue' is the old word clew, a ball of thread: Ariadne's thread led this hero out of the Labyrinth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian slayer of the Minotaur found his way out of the maze by following a ball of thread.
